## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../../assets/interactive/interactive-lessons.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../../assets/interactive/hypothesis-testing-lesson.css">
<div class="clt-lesson ht-lesson"><p>Suppose a researcher wants to know whether college students using a new study strategy have a different average score on a hypothetical attention test. The reference population has a mean of 50 and a known standard deviation of 10. In the study, a sample of 25 students has an average score of 54.</p><p>Could this result reasonably occur if the population mean were still 50? In this optional Week 8 activity, we use the <strong>null distribution</strong> to investigate that question. The example is a statistical comparison to a reference, not proof of a causal treatment effect.</p><div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Interpret a two-sided p-value as a probability under the null model.</li><li>Explain how the distance between an observed sample mean and the null mean affects the p-value.</li><li>Distinguish the p-value from the significance level and explain how they determine a statistical decision.</li><li>Interpret rejection and failure to reject without treating them as proof.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review normal probabilities, sampling distributions, standard error, and confidence intervals.</p></div></div>
~~~

## Make a prediction

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ht-lesson" id="ht-lesson"><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="prediction"><legend>If the observed sample mean moves from 51 to 54, what happens to the two-sided p-value when sample size and SD stay fixed?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-prediction" value="larger"> It becomes larger.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-prediction" value="smaller"> It becomes smaller.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-prediction" value="same"> It stays the same.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check prediction</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><section class="clt-simulator" aria-labelledby="ht-explore"><h2 id="ht-explore">Explore evidence against the null hypothesis</h2><p><strong>Null hypothesis (H₀):</strong> population mean = 50. <strong>Alternative hypothesis (H₁):</strong> population mean ≠ 50.</p><p class="clt-lead">Assume independent observations from a normal population with known SD 10. Change the observed sample mean and sample size to see how unusual the result would be under the null model.</p><div class="clt-controls"><div class="clt-control"><label for="ht-n">Observations per sample (n)</label><select id="ht-n" aria-describedby="ht-n-help"><option value="10">10</option><option value="25" selected>25</option><option value="50">50</option><option value="100">100</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="ht-n-help">Changing sample size clears the simulation.</span></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="ht-alpha">Significance level (α)</label><select id="ht-alpha" aria-describedby="ht-alpha-help"><option value="0.01">0.01</option><option value="0.05" selected>0.05</option><option value="0.10">0.10</option></select><span class="clt-help" id="ht-alpha-help">Choose alpha before examining data in an actual study.</span></div></div><div class="clt-control"><label for="ht-mean">Observed sample mean: <output data-output="mean">54.0</output></label><input id="ht-mean" type="range" min="44" max="56" step="0.1" value="54" aria-describedby="ht-mean-help"><span class="clt-help" id="ht-mean-help">Use the slider or arrow keys. This changes the hypothetical observed result, not the null mean of 50. The same simulated null samples are reclassified.</span></div><div class="ht-metrics"><div class="ht-metric"><span>Observed z-statistic</span><strong data-output="z">—</strong></div><div class="ht-metric"><span>Two-sided p-value</span><strong data-output="p">—</strong></div><div class="ht-metric"><span>Significance level</span><strong data-output="alpha">—</strong></div></div><h3>What outcomes would be at least as extreme?</h3><div class="ht-chart-wrap" data-chart="null"></div><div class="ht-legend"><span><i class="ht-key ht-tail" aria-hidden="true"></i>At least as extreme as observed</span><span><i class="ht-key ht-other" aria-hidden="true"></i>Other outcomes</span></div><p class="clt-help">The shaded tails begin at <strong data-output="cutoffs">—</strong> standard error units. The dot marks the observed z-statistic. Both tails are counted because the alternative allows differences in either direction.</p><table class="clt-summary"><caption>Test calculation</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Standard error (10 / √n)</th><td data-output="se">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="ht-decision" data-output="decision" role="status" aria-live="polite">—</p><p data-output="reason"></p><h3>Compare with repeated studies under the null</h3><p>Imagine drawing many independent samples from a population where the null is true. Each sample contributes one standardized sample mean to the histogram. What fraction is at least as extreme as our hypothetical observed result?</p><div class="clt-action-row" role="group" aria-label="Draw samples under the null"><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-draw="1">Draw 1 sample</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="100">Draw 100 samples</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn" data-draw="1000">Draw 1,000 samples</button><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary" data-action="reset">Reset</button></div><p class="clt-status" data-output="status" role="status" aria-live="polite">Ready. Draw samples to begin.</p><div class="ht-chart-wrap" data-chart="empirical"></div><div class="ht-legend"><span><i class="ht-key ht-tail" aria-hidden="true"></i>At least as extreme</span><span><i class="ht-key ht-other" aria-hidden="true"></i>Other simulated results</span></div><table class="clt-summary"><caption>All simulated null samples</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Total null samples</th><td data-output="count">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">At least as extreme</th><td data-output="extreme">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Observed percentage at least as extreme</th><td data-output="empirical">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Theoretical tail probability (%)</th><td data-output="theoretical">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="clt-caption">The graphs share a horizontal z scale; the curve shows density and the histogram shows counts. The observed fraction estimates the theoretical p-value and varies from run to run. Zero extreme results in a finite simulation does not mean the theoretical probability is zero. A run is limited to 20,000 samples.</p></section></div>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ht-lesson"><ol><li>Start with n = 25, mean = 54, and alpha = 0.05. Predict how many out of 1,000 null samples will be at least as extreme, then draw 1,000 and compare.</li><li>Move the observed mean toward 50, then to 46. How do the two tails and p-value change? Why do 46 and 54 produce the same p-value?</li><li>Set the mean to 54, then compare alpha = 0.05 and 0.01. Does the p-value change? Does the decision change?</li><li>Keep mean = 54, compare n = 10 and 100, and explain why the same difference can provide different evidence as standard error changes.</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> Does a small p-value establish that the study strategy caused a meaningful improvement? What else would you need to know?</p></div>
~~~

## What is a p-value telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ht-lesson"><p>A hypothesis test begins with a model and a question. Here we ask whether the population mean differs from 50. Under H₀, the sampling distribution of sample means is normal with mean 50 and standard error 10 / √n. Standardizing a sample mean expresses its distance from the null mean in standard error units.</p><div class="ht-formula"><strong>One-sample z-test (known SD)</strong><br>z = (observed sample mean − hypothesized mean) / standard error<br>Standard error = σ / √n<br>Two-sided p = P(|Z| ≥ |observed z|), assuming H₀</div><p>At n = 25 and observed mean = 54, the standard error is 2, so z = 2. Under the null model, about 2.28% of results are at or above +2, and about 2.28% are at or below −2. The combined probability is approximately 0.0455. At alpha = 0.05, reject H₀; at alpha = 0.01, fail to reject H₀.</p><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> A sample mean that lies farther into the tails is harder to reconcile with the null model. Larger samples have smaller standard errors; the same difference from 50 therefore becomes more unusual under the null. But the p-value does not measure how large or practically important the effect is, and it is not the probability that H₀ is true.</p><p>For a two-sided z-test, the null mean is outside the matching confidence interval precisely when the test rejects (except for the boundary convention at exact equality). This connects the current activity to Week 7. In real studies we often estimate population variability and use a t-test instead. Statistical power and decision errors will be addressed in the next activity.</p></div>
~~~

## Check your understanding

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ht-lesson" id="ht-knowledge-check"><p>These four questions revisit the learning goals. Your answers stay in your browser.</p><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="meaning"><legend>1. What does a p-value of 0.04 mean?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-meaning" value="null"> There is a 4% probability the null hypothesis is true.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-meaning" value="extreme"> If the null model is true, a statistic at least as extreme as observed occurs with probability 0.04.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-meaning" value="effect"> There is a 96% probability the intervention works.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="distance"><legend>2. At fixed n and population SD, what happens when the observed sample mean moves farther from 50?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-distance" value="same"> The p-value stays the same.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-distance" value="larger"> The p-value increases.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-distance" value="smaller"> The p-value decreases.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="alpha"><legend>3. If an observed p-value is 0.04 and alpha changes from 0.05 to 0.01, what happens?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-alpha" value="unchanged"> The p-value stays 0.04; the decision changes from reject to fail to reject.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-alpha" value="smaller"> The p-value becomes 0.01.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-alpha" value="same"> The decision and p-value both stay the same.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><fieldset class="clt-question" data-question="decision"><legend>4. What does failing to reject the null hypothesis mean?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-decision" value="true"> The null hypothesis has been proven true.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-decision" value="insufficient"> There is insufficient evidence against the null at the chosen significance level.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ht-decision" value="equal"> The observed sample mean must equal 50.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> A p-value quantifies how unusual the observed statistic (or more extreme results) would be under the null model. Alpha is a decision threshold, not the probability that a hypothesis is true.</p><p>Textbook connection: OpenStax <em>Introductory Statistics 2e</em>, Chapter 9, Hypothesis Testing with One Sample.</p></div>
